### 4.4.1 – Writing an Equation From a Graph

* Look for the **y-intercept** first — where the line crosses the y-axis.
* Then find the **slope** by counting rise/run between two points.
* Substitute (m) and (b) into (y = mx + b) (or (f(x) = mx + b)).

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_4/find_equation_from_graph.png){width="340px" fig-align="center"}

:::{.real-world title="Example – Car Rental Costs"}
A company charges $50 plus $0.25 per mile.
The rule is (y = 0.25x + 50).

* (m = 0.25): rate per mile
* (b = 50): starting fee
:::

:::{.you-try title="From Graph to Equation"}
Use the graph your teacher provides. Identify the slope and y-intercept, then write the equation in slope-intercept form.
:::

---

### 4.4.2 – Writing an Equation From Slope and a Point

When you know a line’s slope and one point, use **point-slope form**:
[
y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)
]

Then rearrange to slope-intercept form if needed.

:::{.example title="Example – Point and Slope"}
Slope (m = 3), point ((2, 5)):
[
\begin{align*}
y - 5 &= 3(x - 2) \
y - 5 &= 3x - 6 \
y &= 3x - 1
\end{align*}
]

So (y = 3x - 1) or (f(x) = 3x - 1).
:::

:::{.you-try title="Use Point-Slope Form"}
Find the equation of a line with slope (m = -2) that passes through ((1, 4)). Write your final answer as (y = mx + b).
:::

---

### 4.4.3 – Writing an Equation From Two Points

When you only know **two points**, first find the **slope**:
[
m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}
]

Then use one of the points and point-slope form to find the equation.

:::{.example title="Example – Two Points"}
Points ((1, 2)) and ((4, 5)):

[
m = \frac{5 - 2}{4 - 1} = 1
]

Use point ((1, 2)):
[
y - 2 = 1(x - 1) \implies y = x + 1
]
:::

:::{.you-try-m title="Try It Yourself"}
Find the equation of the line passing through ((–2, 3)) and ((2, 7)).
:::

---

### 4.4.4 – Rearranging Equations Into Slope-Intercept Form

Sometimes a line is written in another form, like (3x + 2y = 10).
To graph it easily, solve for (y).

[
\begin{align*}
3x + 2y &= 10 \
2y &= -3x + 10 \
y &= -\frac{3}{2}x + 5
\end{align*}
]

Now the slope is (-\frac{3}{2}) and the y-intercept is (5).

:::{.you-try title="Put It in Slope-Intercept Form"}
Rewrite (4x - 2y = 6) in slope-intercept form. Identify (m) and (b).
:::

---

### 4.4.5 – Interpreting Slope and Intercept in Context

:::{.real-world title="Example – Earnings Over Time"}
A dog walker earns $15 per walk, plus $10 just for showing up.
The rule is (f(x) = 15x + 10).

* (m = 15): rate (how much per walk)
* (b = 10): base pay
:::

:::{.you-try-m title="Interpret the Meaning"}
You spend $25 to join a club and $5 each visit.
Write an equation for total cost (f(x)).
What do (m) and (b) represent?
:::

:::{.remember title="Key Idea"}
You can write linear equations from graphs, data, or descriptions.
Once you know **slope** and **one point** (or intercept), you can find the rule that models the situation.
:::

:::{.real-world title="Comparing Two Models"}
You track two savings plans:  
\(f(x) = 10x + 100\) and \(g(x) = 20x + 20\).  
Graph both.  
The **intersection point** shows when your total savings are equal.  
That single point satisfies both functions — it’s the **solution to the system**.
:::
